Google will allow some advertisers to show a business name in their ads that does not match the domain the ad sends people to, according to a notice posted on October 1, 2026, in the Google Ads Advertising Policies Help Center. The change, which takes effect in October 2026, applies only when three conditions are met, and it carves out resellers, independent booking intermediaries, affiliate distributors and secondary sellers entirely.
In Short
Google Ads used to want the business name shown in an ad to line up with the website the ad points to, but now a company can show a different name if it really is that brand and has a checked link to whoever owns the website. This matters for businesses that sell through a website owned by a parent company, a partner or a brand they belong to. Middlemen who just resell other people's products, rooms or services still cannot put the brand's name alone in that field.
What the notice says
The notice is titled "Update to Editorial Policy (October 2026)" and sits in the change log of Google's advertising policies. Its substance concerns a single requirement within the Editorial policy: the rules governing the business name field that appears alongside many Google ad formats.
According to Google, "In October 2026, Google will update its Business name requirements policy to allow for differences between the business name and the destination domain in certain limited cases." The notice lists the three conditions an advertiser has to satisfy. The business name must accurately reflect "the recognized name or brand of the advertiser." There must be "a verified direct relationship between the advertiser and the domain owner." And "the advertiser's products or services are directly offered in the destination domain."
The exclusion follows in a separate paragraph. "Third-party resellers, independent booking intermediaries, affiliate distributors, and secondary sellers do not qualify for this provision and are prohibited from using the standalone brand name of the goods, services, or properties they offer as their business name," the notice states.
That is the entire policy text. It runs to two paragraphs and a bulleted list, followed by the line "(Posted on October 1, 2026)."
The AI summary and the missing answers
The help page carries a block labelled "Summarized by Google AI" and marked as a beta. It condenses the change into two sentences: "Starting October 2026, Google will allow business names to differ from destination domains under specific conditions. Advertisers must maintain a verified relationship with the domain owner and accurately reflect their recognized brand name."
Below it, the page offers three suggested questions to put to a support agent. One of them is "What proof is needed to verify the advertiser and domain relationship?" The policy text itself does not answer it. Nowhere in the notice does Google describe what counts as a "verified direct relationship," which documents or account links establish one, or whether the check runs through the existing advertiser verification programme or through a new process.
The notice also gives a month rather than a day. Search Engine Roundtable reported on October 2, 2026 that a Google email shared by an advertiser put the start date at October 16, 2026. The help page itself says only October 2026.
How the rule worked before
The business name requirement is short, but it has been one of the more frequent sources of disapprovals in search advertising, because the field is mandatory in several formats and is checked against something external: the landing page domain or the name an advertiser has verified with Google.
According to Google's current Business name requirements page, the field may contain the domain, the advertiser's recognized name, or the name of an advertised downloadable app. Generic or location-based names are not allowed, and neither is promotional language placed in the name field. The page sets a 25-character limit. Advertisers that have gone through advertiser verification can use the domain or the name they submitted during verification, and those whose legal name does not match or runs longer than 25 characters can pursue Brand Verification if they hold an active trademark registration.
Resellers and authorized dealers already had a defined route under the existing page. They could add qualifying language to the name, such as a dealer name followed by a location. The October text keeps that logic and sharpens it: a reseller cannot use the brand name on its own.
Enforcement is not immediate. Google's existing page says a warning is issued at least seven days before an account is suspended for violations of this policy, and that edited ads are re-reviewed, typically within 24 to 48 hours. PPC Land covered Google's April 2025 clarification that repeat violations trigger a warning at least seven days before suspension, while egregious violations lead to immediate suspension.
The last time Google revised the Editorial policy wholesale, in May 2024, PPC Land reported that the update was presented as a rewrite for clarity with no change in enforcement scope. That version said business names displayed in ads must accurately reflect the advertiser, the advertised app or the domain associated with the landing page. The October 2026 change is different in kind: it creates a new permitted case rather than restating an old one.
Who the change is for
Google does not name industries or give examples, so the following is inference from the wording rather than anything Google has stated.
The three conditions describe an advertiser whose own brand is genuine, whose products are sold on someone else's domain, and whose connection to that domain's owner is formal. Several familiar structures fit. A subsidiary that sells through a parent group's website is one. A franchisee or a property operator selling rooms on a hotel chain's booking site is another. A brand whose online store runs on a domain held by a holding company or a licensing partner would also appear to qualify.
Under the old rule, each of these advertisers faced an awkward choice. They could show the domain owner's name, which might be a holding company that consumers have never heard of. They could show their own brand and risk disapproval because the name did not match the domain. Or they could go through Brand Verification, which requires an active trademark.
The vocabulary of the exclusion points in the same direction. "Independent booking intermediaries" and the phrase "goods, services, or properties" both suggest that Google drafted the rule with travel and accommodation in mind, where the line between a hotel advertising its own rooms and a third-party site selling those same rooms has long been contested in paid search. The word "properties" in particular has little application outside lodging and real estate.
The exclusion list
Four categories are excluded by name: third-party resellers, independent booking intermediaries, affiliate distributors and secondary sellers.
The common thread is that none of them is the brand. A reseller sells another company's goods. A booking intermediary sells another company's rooms, seats or tickets. An affiliate distributor earns a commission for sending customers to someone else. A secondary seller trades goods that have already passed through the primary market.
The notice does not merely say these businesses fail to qualify. It adds that they are "prohibited from using the standalone brand name of the goods, services, or properties they offer as their business name." The word "standalone" is doing work here. Read alongside the existing reseller provision, it leaves room for qualifying language, so a name built from the brand plus a word that signals the advertiser's own role appears to remain possible, while the brand name by itself does not.
There is a definitional gap. The notice does not define what makes a booking intermediary "independent." Many hotels sign distribution contracts with the platforms that sell their rooms, so what separates an independent intermediary from a contracted one? Google does not say. In practice the question may matter less than it appears: a booking platform advertising its own site is both the advertiser and the domain owner, so the new provision, which covers advertisers sending traffic to a domain someone else owns, would not reach it. What the notice does make explicit is that the platform cannot use the hotel's name on its own.
Where the field appears
The business name field is shown in several Google Ads formats, including search ads that carry a business name asset and campaigns such as Performance Max, where Google assembles ads automatically from assets supplied by the advertiser. Google's existing requirements page states that the policy applies to ad formats that require a business name field. The October notice does not narrow or extend that scope, so the new provision should apply wherever the existing rule did.
That matters because the business name is one of the few pieces of text in an automated ad that is anchored to identity rather than to the product. In formats where Google mixes headlines, descriptions and images at serving time, the business name and the displayed domain are the signals a user has to judge who is behind an ad. Allowing them to diverge, even in limited cases, means the two signals will sometimes name different entities by design.
Context: identity and enforcement
The change lands in a period when Google has tied more of its advertising rules to verified identity.
Google extended advertiser identity verification beyond political advertisers to all advertisers in 2020, requiring legal names that match registration documents. It then rolled the programme out country by country, including a batch of 51 countries in January 2022. In December 2023, it expanded verification to trade names and "doing business as" names, as long as the legal name and the trade name appear together on the supporting documents. In November 2025, PPC Land reported that Google added language making clear that false verification information leads to suspension without prior warning.
Impersonation sits close to the same territory. In February 2024, Google tightened its Misrepresentation policy against ads that impersonate brands or falsely imply affiliation, with violations leading to immediate suspension. The October 2026 business name provision addresses the legitimate counterpart of that problem: an advertiser that genuinely is affiliated with a brand, but whose website sits on someone else's domain.
The scale of enforcement explains why the field matters. PPC Land reported in September 2026 that Google suspended about 24.9 million advertiser accounts worldwide in 2025, down from 39.2 million in 2024, and blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion ads. Google has also linked serving limits to identity: in June 2026 it extended its limited ad serving policy to Google Search, restricting impressions for advertisers it does not yet consider established.
Against that background, a provision that loosens a name-matching rule is unusual. It runs against the general direction of travel, which has been toward fewer discrepancies between what an ad says and who stands behind it. The counterweight is the word "verified." Google is not allowing names to diverge freely; it is allowing them to diverge where it can confirm a relationship.
What remains unclear
Several practical questions are left open by the notice.
Verification mechanism. The policy depends on "a verified direct relationship," but the notice does not say who verifies it or how. It could rely on documents submitted through advertiser verification, on account-level links between the advertiser and the domain owner, or on something new. Until Google publishes that detail, it is not clear how an advertiser would demonstrate eligibility before an ad is reviewed.
Recognized name. The first condition requires that the name reflect "the recognized name or brand of the advertiser." The existing policy already uses the idea of a recognized name, but the notice does not say whether recognition is assessed through Brand Verification, trademark registration, or reviewer judgment.
Effective date. The help page says October 2026. A specific day, October 16, has been reported from a Google email rather than from the policy page.
Interaction with the 25-character limit. The notice does not alter the existing limit, so advertisers with long brand names would still face the same constraint.
Effect on the main policy page. As of the posting, the change log entry describes the update. Whether and when the Business name requirements page itself will carry the new exception is not stated in the notice.
Why this matters for advertisers
For brands that sell through a parent company's site, a franchise system's booking engine or a partner's storefront, the change removes a mismatch that the previous rule forced on them. They will be able to show the name consumers actually recognize, provided they can satisfy whatever verification Google applies.
For intermediaries, the effect points the other way. The explicit prohibition on standalone brand names leaves less ambiguity than before about whether a booking site or an affiliate can present itself under the name of the property or product it sells. In categories such as hotels, where intermediaries and property owners frequently compete for the same queries, the difference between a brand name with and without qualifying language is visible to every user who sees the ad.
The policy also adds one more step in which Google, rather than the advertiser, decides which relationships count. That pattern has repeated across verification, impersonation and limited ad serving. Each time, the practical outcome has depended less on the published text than on how reviewers and automated systems apply it. With only two paragraphs of policy to go on and no published verification process, that will again be the case here.

- May 2020 - Google extends identity verification to all advertisers, requiring legal names that match registration documents.
- January 27, 2022 - Google begins requesting verification from advertisers in 51 more countries.
- November 21, 2023 - Misleading representation violations move under the Unacceptable business practices policy.
- December 2023 - Google expands advertiser verification to trade names and DBAs.
- March 2024 - Google's impersonation update to the Misrepresentation policy takes effect, with immediate suspension for violations.
- May 2024 - Google rewrites the Editorial policy for clarity, keeping the rule that business names must reflect the advertiser, app or landing page domain.
- April 7, 2025 - Google clarifies account suspension policies, including a warning at least seven days before suspension for repeat violations.
- November 4, 2025 - Google adds language on false verification information to its Circumventing systems policy.
- June 12, 2026 - Google extends limited ad serving to Google Search.
- September 15, 2026 - Analysis of Google's 2025 enforcement data shows 24.9 million advertiser accounts suspended worldwide.

- October 2, 2026 - Search Engine Roundtable reports a Google email giving October 16, 2026, as the start date.
- October 2026 - The business name exception takes effect, according to Google.

Summary
Who: Google, through its Google Ads Advertising Policies Help Center, affecting advertisers whose brand differs from the owner of the domain their ads point to, and excluding third-party resellers, independent booking intermediaries, affiliate distributors and secondary sellers.
What: An update to the Business name requirements within Google's Editorial policy that allows the business name in an ad to differ from the destination domain when the name reflects the advertiser's recognized brand, the advertiser has a verified direct relationship with the domain owner, and its products or services are offered directly on that domain. Excluded categories are prohibited from using the standalone brand name of what they sell.
When: Posted on October 1, 2026, taking effect in October 2026. Search Engine Roundtable reported a Google email giving October 16, 2026.
Where: Google Ads formats that carry a business name field, globally, as the notice names no regional limits.
Why: The previous rule required the business name to match the domain, the advertiser's recognized name or a verified name, which left brands selling on a parent's or partner's domain without a clean option. Google has not explained how it will verify the advertiser-domain relationship the new provision depends on.
